title: Last words
hook: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah enters the garden (Abu Dawud)
carry: let these be my last words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shia adhan, and your line: the call, as each hears it. Did you listen to both calls, and hear what each one carries? Today the testimony reaches its last word. Day one thousand seventy-two.

A room late at night, the lamp turned low. An old woman in the bed, her breathing slow and uneven. Her son sits close and, every so often, without any pressure in his voice, says the same few words near her ear: la ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. He isn't quizzing her. He's leaving the words in the air, the way you'd leave a light on in the hallway, in case she wants to reach for them. Then he goes quiet again, and the room holds the words with him. Today, the end of the line.
screen: `A LAMP TURNED LOW.` → `A FEW WORDS, NEAR HER EAR.` → `A LIGHT LEFT ON IN THE HALLWAY.`

segments.voice: The son in that room is following two sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The first is in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 3116: whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter the garden. The second is in Sahih Muslim, number 916: prompt your dying with la ilaha illallah. The word for that gentle prompting is talqin. Scholars who explain it advise doing it softly, to say the words rather than order the dying person to repeat them, and not to keep pressing if they've already said them. The point is an open door, not a test. Now turn it around. Nobody chooses the hour. So how does anyone make sure of their last words? Sahih al-Bukhari, number 247, gives one answer. The Prophet ﷺ told a companion: when you go to bed, make wudu as you would for prayer, lie on your right side, and say a short supplication handing yourself over to God. If you die that night, he said, you die on the natural way, and he told him to make those words the last thing he said. So the habit of bedtime becomes a rehearsal. Sleep, in this teaching, is a small cousin of death; the Qur'an speaks of God taking souls at the time of their death, and of those that have not died, in their sleep. That's 39:42. Some Muslims join these teachings and say the shahada as the very last thing before sleep, night after night, so the words are well worn by the time they're needed. This also closes our days on the testimony: two sentences, a no and a yes, the messenger, what it asks, oneness, and now the last place those two sentences go.
screen: `PROMPT YOUR DYING, SOFTLY.` · `AN OPEN DOOR, NOT A TEST.` · `NOBODY CHOOSES THE HOUR.` · `BEDTIME AS A REHEARSAL.` · then, large: `LA ILAHA ILLALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a rehearsal for tonight. Sit or lie the way you might at bedtime. Let the day go out of your shoulders. Think of what you'd want your last words to be, not in drama, just honestly. If you're Muslim and you pray, you can say la ilaha illallah slowly, once, and then let the quiet hold it. If you're not, you can sit with the question the son in that room was answering: what words do I want close by at the end? Keep breathing. Nothing to fix tonight. The bell holds the time.
Last words. In this teaching, the shahada said at the end, prompted gently by those who love you, and rehearsed every night before sleep. Today's word.

Your line: let these be my last words. Tonight, make the last thing you say before sleep something you'd be glad to end on. Tomorrow, the prayer begins, with what comes before it. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Muslims at a deathbed often say la ilaha illallah softly near the dying person, a practice called talqin, and some say the shahada or the bedtime supplication taught in the hadith as the last words before sleep.

pairs: souls taken at death and in sleep

myth: talqin means pressing the dying person to repeat the words
scholars who explain it say to say the words softly, not to order or keep pressing.
a hadith ties bedtime words to dying on the natural way
Bukhari 247: if you die that night after saying them, you die on the natural way.
the Qur'an links sleep and death in one verse
39:42 speaks of souls taken at death, and of those not yet dead, in their sleep.

fork.setup: you're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and you want to help them with the words la ilaha illallah. what does the teaching on talqin suggest?
options: ask them again and again to repeat it.
say it softly near them, and don't keep pressing.
stay silent, since it's not your place.
fork.reveal: talqin is a gentle prompt: say the words softly, leave them in the air, and stop pressing once they've said them.

original.note: Arabic: there is no god but Allah, the first half of the shahada.

trapdoor: what you thought: last words are whatever someone happens to say.
what it means: in this teaching, the shahada at the end, prompted softly by family and rehearsed each night.
what a scholar hears: talqin of the dying (Muslim 916) and the bedtime habit of Bukhari 247, read together with 39:42 on sleep and death.

notes: Hadith numbers to confirm: Abu Dawud 3116 (Mu'adh ibn Jabal, last words la ilaha illallah); Muslim 916 (laqqinu mawtakum); Bukhari 247 (al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, bedtime wudu and du'a, 'make them your last words', die 'ala al-fitrah).
Talqin etiquette (softly, not ordering, not repeating once said) is described from the fiqh manuals generally; no specific source cited. Confirm.
Bukhari 247's supplication is not the shahada; the script says only that 'some Muslims' join the two teachings by saying the shahada before sleep (the outline's practice). Confirm the framing.
